doc.title: Jane Ira Bloom interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 3, 1998

title: Closing thoughts on talking about music
summary: Words can't capture the music; that's why we play instead of talk.

story.theme_name: Thanks and goodbyes: closing the interview
story.community_name: Closing the interview: thanks, goodbyes and tape running out

blocks.x: Right. Well I want to thank you for your time today, and I hope that if I haven’t asked you anything that you had on your mind —

Well let me think about that for a minute. Well you know here’s something, this is interesting, I mean to put on a videotape. Because when you have these kind of talks and you’re trying to talk about music and get these issues sort of out, it makes it seem as if it’s clear what you do and what you think. I think I always like to make sure that after I have one of these experiences that whoever I’m talking to — you at the time — or whoever’s listening to this videotape, that the words that were used to describe what we do help us understand things but it’s not the thing itself. And I always worry that talking so much about it may demystify something about the ambiguity of what we do. It’s so, I am sitting here trying to put it into words but it doesn’t exist in that realm in my mind. And so it’s like a conscious effort to talk to you about it. I’m using a different part of my brain to do it, and the part of my brain that plays music and lives in that music world. And I guess I always like to just leave with the thought that it’s much more ambiguous and abstract and emotional and passionate thing that we’re talking about than these words convey. And that’s why we play instead of talk.
The answer in on your records not in talking about them. Yeah.
Well that’s a good statement to make and I’m glad you said that, that talking about it only goes so far. Do you have any other passions besides music? Hobbies?
